tyāga
(‘giving up’)
------------------------------------------
Tyāga or giving up is an important concept found in the Hindu scriptures.
It has two aspects: giving away something to someone who needs it more; giving up an object feeling that it is not a necessity or even an obstacle to the way of life one has chosen.
The former is known as दान (See DĀNA for details.) and the latter as वैराग्य (renunciation). दान has been prescribed as a duty for the householders. वैराग्य is an essential qualification for one who aspires after सṁन्यास or monastic life.
The Manusmṛti (8.389) forbids a householder from giving up his parents, wife and sons who depend upon him.
The Bhagavadgītā (18.2) gives a general definition of त्याग as giving up the fruits of all actions. It then categorises the त्याग of actions into three types: sāttvika, rājasika and tāmasika.
Sāttvika-त्याग consists in performing one’s prescribed duties but giving up attachment towards them as also the fruits thereof.
Giving up one’s prescribed duties because they entail a lot of physical exertion is rājasika-त्याग.
If the same is done out of delusion or confused understanding, it is tāmasika-त्याग (vide Bhagavadgītā 18.7-9).
The Bhagavadgītā, however, unequivocally declares that works like यज्ञ (sacrifice), दान (giving gifts) and तपस् (austerities) should not be given up, but, must be performed. They always have a purifying effect.

------------------------------------------
Tyāgarāja is one of the all-time great musician saints of India. The Carnatic music—classical मुसिच् of South Indian tradition—has been immensely benefited and enriched by his soulful compositions. Side by side, he also contributed greatly to the cult of devotion to राम.
Tyāgarāja was born in A.

at Tiruvārūr in the Tañjāvūr (Tanjore) district of Tamil Nadu in a Telugu-speaking ब्राह्मण family. His parents were Rāmabrahma and Sītāmbā. Since Tiruvārūr was famous for its temple of Lord शिव, known as Tyāgarājasvāmin, the boy was named Tyāgarājabrahma.
Later on, the family shifted to Tiruvayyār, also called Pañcanadakṣetra.
Tyāgarāja was given a good एदुचतिओन् especially in Sanskrit and Telugu. He also became proficient in some other fields of knowledge like the वेदस्, पुराणस्, ज्यौतिष (astrology) and gaṇita (mathematics).
He was initiated by one Rāmakṛṣṇā-nandasvāmin with a special मन्त्र of राम.
TyāgarājaEndowed with a good voice and memory, त्यागराज had a flair for मुसिच्. The devotional songs of पुरन्दरदास (A.

-1687) and others, which his मोथेर् used to sing, deeply influenced him. He started composing songs even from a young-age.
Recognising his talents, his ड़थेर् arranged for his मुसिच्-training under Soṇṭhi Veṅkaṭaramaṇayya, the topmost musician of his times. Very soon, he excelled in it.
He is said to have been blessed by the sage नारद who came disguised as a saṁnyāsin and left an ancient treatise on music—the Svarārṇava—with him. त्यागराज mastered it very soon.
He was married to पार्वती, at the age of eighteen. After her early demise, he married her younger sister Kamalā.
Tyāgarāja was once blessed by a sage who advised him to repeat Rāmanāma (mantra of राम) 96 crore times, which he did faithfully, completing it in about twenty-one years. He succeeded in getting a vision of Śrī राम several times.
He is supposed to have composed 24,000 songs though only 800 are available now.
He lived by उञ्छवृत्ति (gathering corn left in agricultural fields). The people of the town who respected him greatly, also supported him. Though kings and noblemen invited him to their courts he flatly refused their invitations.
Only once, he went on a पिल्ग्रिमगे to a few places in South India, like तिरुपति, Kāñcipuram, मदुरै and श्रीरङ्गम्.
Though a few miracles, like bringing back a dead person to life, have been attributed to him, he considered them as having happened by the grace of राम.
He took सṁन्यास during the last days and passed away peacefully while his disciples were chanting the name of राम.
His songs—most of which are in Telugu and a few in Sanskrit—though imbued with intense devotional fervour, are also classics even from the standpoint of literary merit.
His other compositions are: Prahlāda-bhaktivijayam, Naukācaritram and Sītā-rāmavijayam. These are called geya-nāṭakas, which can be enacted as dramas with plenty of मुसिच्.
His गुरुकुल (traditional academy for teaching) produced a good number of great musicians who continued his tradition of मुसिच्.
His समाधि (the place where his body has been interred) has been well-preserved even today. The day of his passing away (called puṇyārādhana) is observed with special worship and singing of his songs by great musicians.
